hints: Look carefully at the enlarged view on the right. Which label points to the ball of histones, which points to the thread wrapping around it, and which points to the single small histone at the base?
Remember what has to happen in prophase of mitosis. The loose beads-on-a-string must pack much tighter to make a short, thick chromatid visible under the microscope.
walkthrough:
**Identify P, Q and R from the diagram**

Lovely, let us start by reading the picture. P points to the cluster of round balls in the centre. That is the histone octamer core.

Q points to the thin thread winding around those balls. That is the DNA molecule. R points to the single flattened protein at the bottom where DNA enters and leaves. That is the linker histone H1.

**Recall the nucleosome unit**

Think beads on a string. DNA (Q) wraps about twice around the core of 8 histones (P), and is locked in place by the linker histone (R). Together this makes a nucleosome, the basic packing unit of chromatin.

**Apply this to prophase**

In interphase the string is loose so genes can be used. In prophase of mitosis the whole string of nucleosomes coils, folds and supercoils further and further. This condensation forms the thick, short chromatid we see as a mitotic chromosome. That is exactly what option D describes.

options.A: This swaps P and R. DNA (Q) wraps around the core histones (P), not R, and is held in place by the linker histone (R), not P.
options.B: Nucleosomes do move closer during condensation, but they do not condense around R. R is just the small linker histone, not a scaffold for the whole chromosome.
options.C: It is true histones are protein and help DNA fit in the nucleus, but R is not wrapped by DNA like P is. Also this does not describe the extra folding into a chromatid that happens in prophase.
options.D: Correct. In prophase the chain of nucleosomes made of P plus R plus Q coils and folds repeatedly to form the highly condensed chromatid.
